Bought this from the apple store. I've used many other screen protectors in the past, but thought this would be a step up, as it is manufactured by 3M. Unfortunately, it seems I should have stuck with one of the other screen protector specialists.

The application should be relatively easy, except that it is really difficult to adjust the screen protector once you've started applying it to the phone (compare with some of the other applicators which allow you to start again if needed). Also, the iphone screen was perfectly clean (brand new iphone that I only took out the packaging moments before trying to apply the screen protector), but the applicator still had patches where the protector did not adhere to the screen, leaving bubbles. Also, the squeegee provided was a weak piece of cardboard; others provide stiffer plastic pieces.

Finally, the protector is not as well as you would have thought. It does fit, but fits loosely (i.e. the cut outs for the home button and the speaker/front camera are larger than those in other screen protectors). This is helpful when applying the protector, but looks a little budget when compared with other screen protectors available for less on amazon.

All in all, this is not a product that can compete with even some of the much cheaper screen protectors designed for this version of iPhone.

The T-Mobile Shadow is visually a gorgeous phone, however it has some serious flaws. First, here's the good news:

It has the standard features of most smartphones out now: camera, music player, speakerphone, IM capabilities, internet access. It's not as big as T-Mobile's Wing or Sidekick, and you can hold it one hand and do what you need to do. Like a Blackberry, it has a wonderful QWERTY keyboard that allows me to send text messages and email pretty quickly. You can program it to receive mail (be it AOL, Hotmail, Gmail, your internet service provider, company intranet, etc.) through Outlook. The screen is large and the display is beautiful, bright and easy to read - which is a relief for those who have to wear glasses (like me) in order to see some of the smaller text (you can adjust the font size as well). I have the MyFaves plan, so I have those five folks who I call the most in a little circle on the home screen - I love that. It has many other functions that I really don't use that much or at all, but it is basically like carrying a mini-PC in your pocket. It is powered by Windows Mobile, and you'd think it should be everything that anyone who wants and needs to stay connected to the web...but it isn't.

The bad news is that as efficient as this phone is, there are several annoying things about it that prevents me from rating it more than just the three stars I gave it - and with that, I was being generous. T-Mobile is tagging this "the official phone of fun" but with all these glitches, I don't see anything funny about it.

Number 1: BATTERY LIFE IS HORRIBLE!! This, by far, is the biggest drawback with this phone. You should expect a battery to hold a full charge for a good part of the day, but this one doesn't. I thought the battery life on the RAZR was bad, but the Shadow is far worse. Charge the battery all night and the next day you'll see what I mean. If you make a couple of phone calls, check your email, surf the web for a little while, listen to some music and perhaps take a picture, half of your power will be GONE - I'm dead serious. Even though it comes with stereo earbuds, I wouldn't recommend anyone counting on using the music player to replace their iPod. If you are planning to go anywhere for longer than four or five hours, BRING ALONG YOUR CHARGER OR AN EXTRA BATTERY because this phone will die on you. It won't take you through the day unless you recharge it two or three times.

Number 2: This is really related to Number 1, but I'll mention it here because it is vital information for anyone who has this phone. At the end of each function you use, you need to go to the Task Manager to quit the application - be it answering a phone call, sending or answering an email or text, or something as simple as using the calculator or looking at your calendar. If you don't, it will continue to run in the background and sap even more power from the battery. It doesn't matter if you're no longer using that particular application - even after closing all functions, the battery doesn't hold much of a charge. And don't even think about keeping your Wi-Fi or Bluetooth on - those will drain your battery faster than anything!

Number 3: The 2 megapixel camera takes decent pictures, but the photos have a dull, washed-out and yellowish-beige tint to them, no matter how you adjust the camera function - the pics look old and faded. There is no flash or light included, so if you take a pic in a dim room, it's going to come out looking very dark. I took some photos with this camera phone and they were pretty sharp but the color was completely off. In order to fix them, I had to upload them to my computer and work on them via Photoshop - not something I should have to do with all the money I spent on this phone.

Number 4: The speaker sounds very tinny and scratchy.

Number 5: Many of the links in the emails are not clickable, so you still would have to go to your computer to access these. This is yet another thing that does not make this phone "mobile". Also connecting to the internet can be sluggish at times, which I heard has more to do with the Windows Mobile OS through T-Mobile installed on this phone.

Number 6: The phone has the tendency to freeze up and you have to remove the battery to reset it.

In sound setting, for audio, the JBT800 shows as headphone and as headset. Only 'headphone' actually provides any sound when tested (through the settings test mechanism). Selecting 'headset' cause no audio (unless I disable the headset for input). And when I select 'headset' for input (aka mic), and 'headphone' for audio then I get no audio.

I have tried all different combinations of settings and finally found what works. So for those of trying to use this. here is what I had to do.
In sound settings, select 'jbt800 headphones' for audio.
Leave your input (mic) as its built-in mic.
Now go to advanced settings (make sure the app you want to use the headset to running), the app will appear. Select 'headphone' for output and headset as input.

I was using Microsoft Camera (taking video) app as my testing tool.

Next is to get this to work with vmware. On my thin client, I left the audio as headphone and input as default built in. Then in advanced app, I selected vmware and set it to output of speakers (but it comes through the headset) and input of headset. The input is sometimes robotic sounding and not the best quality, but at least it works. The trick seems to be you can never have theJBT800 (either headphone or headset) selected as both input and output.

Overall, I had to jump through hoops to get this to function. Not sure if this is better or worse than other headsets as this is the only bluetooth headset I have, the others are wired usb.

However, since the phone's bezel is curved along its sides (Samsumg Galaxy S8+), the case is designed to allow full use of the screen, which allows me to place it in the stand horizontally (landscape mode).

This is also important because I use earphones to listen to music throughout the day. I'd prefer to have the phone in portrait mode since the AOD (always-on display) does not rotate, but that is not a major issue. What does matter, though, is that Samsung decided to move the earphone jack from the top of the device on my Galaxy S4 that it replaced, to the bottom left corner, which interferes with this stand and also makes me put the phone in my pocket upside-down when listening to it as I move about. That is an issue with the phone's design, not the stand's.

If the bottom fingers of the stand allowed for a slightly fatter phone case rather than just the phone itself, then I could place mine on this stand in portrait mode were it not for the placement of the earphone jack. Well, it seems that this device is the "A" model and the newer "A1" model (for about the same price!) has slightly deeper fingers but it isn't available in the red color. The new model's fingers are 18 mm deep vs. 14 mm, or o.7" vs. o.55", or between 2/3" and 3/4" vs. just over 1/2".

I like that the angle is adjustable so I can keep the overhead lights from reflecting into my eyes. It also allows me to have the phone in portrait mode and just tip it back a bit to keep it from falling out, so having deeper fingers isn't really needed, but I still think I might consider the A1 if I get any more.

The stand's arms have 4 small, well-placed pads to keep the phone from slipping around, plus there are 4 more as feet to keep it from slipping around at my workstation.

While the advert image shows a cord coming through the back of the stand, I don't use it that way since I rarely need to charge my phone during the day, and placing the earphone cord through it would not work for me, either. Having the phone in landscape mode, I have the cord coming off the right side while the stand is on my left, keeping it neatly away from my mouse pad.

I ordered red because I didn't want the standard black or gray. I wanted something with a bit more character to look at while still keeping its pleasant form and functional design.

The stand is made from aluminum (possibly anodized, not sure) with a neatly engraved logo. It is smooth and has no rough edges. The hinge is tight, moves smoothly, and keeps its adjustment with the phone in place. Overall I find nothing objectionable with this stand, and even appreciate how nicely they've designed and built it!

I'm considering buying another one or two for myself at home, but the jury's still out. I may consider the A1 version but I'd like to see it available in red, deep green, and/or cobalt blue, but that's just because I like colors in my life. With a color choice like that I would surely buy one or more.

I just installed this on my Note 9. A lot of the reviews are suspect, from duplicate names, none are verified purchases, and as usual mixing lots of products. I took a chance anyway. Overall, for an inexpensive product, It wasn't the worst, but has issues and one of the two protectors was faulty. I'd give 3 stars or more for the price if they were both good out of the box.

PROS
+Cheap price
+Decent optical clarity
+Not a bad surface feel with finger or S pen
+Adhesive on most of the glass unlike some with only tiny edges (see below).

CONS
-Doesn't cover top strip of the screen near sensors.

-Holds fingerprints. This is minor worry in exchange for the scratch and slight drop protection you install these for.

-Adhesive doesn't cover the entire glass, stops a fraction away from the long edges. This leaves a tiny line you can see of refracted light at the sides of the screen. This also will let dust/liquid get up under that tiny edge as it is right over the curved part of your screen.

-Weak adhesive. The first one didn't stay down right away despite taking great care to install with everything clean and perfect placement. Fairly certain the adhesive is not applied uniformly perfect. I tried squeegee the gap down with microfiber, I even tried applied minor heat with blow dryer. Would not stay, had to remove. Second one went down much better, and only has one small area that raises up. Think I can live with it.

-Glass could be stronger. This glass just doesn't seem to be as strong as the tablet protector glass I just installed.

All in all, this product has potential especially for the price. If you read about these, all brands have issues especially with these curved screens. Would like to see the quality control improve, and the design be tweaked.
